sentences.text: Corythosaurus is a genus of dinosaur whose name means "helmeted lizard," derived from the Greek word for a Corinthian helmet.
This animal reached an estimated length of 7.7 to 9 meters and possessed a skull with a crest that stood 70.8 centimeters tall.
The discovery of the holotype — the specimen the species is based on — was notable for preserving impressions of much of the creature's skin.
Barnum Brown described Corythosaurus in 1914 after discovering the first specimen, AMNH 5240, in 1911 along the Red Deer River of Alberta.
He named the type species Corythosaurus casuarius in 1914 based on a specimen he collected in 1912, which was found in the Belly River Group.
Corythosaurus is classified as a lambeosaurine, a subgroup of hadrosaurid dinosaurs.
A preserved specimen contained conifer needles, seeds, twigs, and fruits, suggesting Corythosaurus fed on these plant materials.
Researchers suggest the crest functioned like a trombone to amplify sound waves produced by exhalation, making vocalization the most likely function of the structure.
Ossified tendons were present on all vertebrae of Corythosaurus except those in the neck region.

The type species of the genus Corythosaurus is Corythosaurus casuarius, while other species once assigned to it include C. intermedius, originally named Stephanosaurus, and C. stebingeri, originally named H. stebingeri.
Corythosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous epoch, specifically the Campanian age, from approximately 77 to 75.7 million years ago.

Based on Late Cretaceous climate conditions, researchers suggest Corythosaurus was a selective feeder that ate the juiciest fruits and youngest leaves, with C. casuarius living from about 77 to 76.5 million years ago in the Oldman Formation.
Research suggests that differences in skull size and shape among Corythosaurus species may be related to sex and age rather than distinct species.

It is debated regarding the anatomy of the crest, as Barnum Brown incorrectly identified the praemaxillae as nasals, leading to errors about their extent and separation, and many presumed traits of the snout described by Brown are incorrect due to this confusion.
Many postcranial traits once thought unique to Corythosaurus are now known to be shared with other lambeosaurines.
